eohippus.e: Originally a genus name, Eohippus, formed in New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”). By surface analysis, eo- + Latin hippus.

s.d: earliest horse; extinct primitive dog-sized four-toed Eocene animal
An extinct early Eocene mammal (Hyracotherium leporinum), ancestral to the modern horse.
x: An eohippus may "evolve" into a horse, but when we say that a society of hunters and gatherers evolves into a farming village, we are using the word "evolves" as a metaphor for a process of directional change.

s.d: a crude stone artifact (as a chipped flint); possibly the earliest tools
Crudely chopped flints, believed to be naturally produced by geological processes such as glaciation.

eolithic.e: From French éolithique; from Ancient Greek Ἠώς (Ēṓs, “dawn”) + λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + -ic. By surface analysis, eo- + lith- + -ic.

s.d: of or relating to the earliest period of the Stone Age (characterized by the use of eoliths)
having properties with different values along different axes

eon.e: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

s.d: the longest division of geological time
an immeasurably long period of time
(Gnosticism) a divine power or nature emanating from the Supreme Being and playing various roles in the operation of the universe
Eternity, the duration of the universe.
A period of one billion (short scale, i.e. 1,000,000,000) years; a gigayear.
The longest geochronologic unit, being a period of hundreds of millions of years; subdivided into eras.
A spirit being emanating from the Godhead.

eonian.e: From Ancient Greek αἰώνιος (aiṓnios, “lasting for an age; perpetual; eternal”) + -an, the former from αἰών (aiṓn, “lifetime; aeon; age; generation”) (whence also eon, aeon) + -ιος (-ios, adjective suffix).

s.d: of or relating to a geological eon (longer than an era)
continuing forever or indefinitely
x: the ageless themes of love and revenge

s.d: Of or pertaining to an eon
eon-long, everlasting
x:
But I should turn mine ears and hear
The moanings of the homeless sea,
⁠The sound of streams that swift or slow
⁠Draw down Æonian hills, and sow
The dust of continents to be; […]

s.d: an older other woman, especially a sister, used by a female
a theropod dinosaur of the genus Eoraptor

eosin.e: Borrowed from German Eosin, coined by Heinrich Caro, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in.

s.d: a red fluorescent dye resulting from the action of bromine on fluorescein; used in cosmetics and as a biological stain for studying cell structures
(uncountable) A red, acidic dye commonly used in histological stains.
x: Eosins are acid xanthene or phthalein dyes. Eosin Y, eosin B, phloxine and erythrosin (which unlike other eosins, is halogenated with iodine), are the common members of this group of dyes.
The hematoxylin and eosin stain (H&E) is the most widely used histological stain.

s.d: a decrease in the number of eosinophils in the blood
(uncountable) A form of agranulocytosis where the number of eosinophil granulocytes is lower than expected.

eosinophil.e: From German eosinophil, from eosin (“rose dye, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in”) + -o- + -phil.

s.d: a leukocyte readily stained with eosin
A white blood cell responsible for combating parasitic infections in the body.
a leukocyte readily stained with eosin

eosinophilia.e: Coined 1879 by American biologist Paul Ehrlich from eosin (“rosy, dawn-colored”) + -o- + -philia. By surface analysis, eosinophil + -ia.

s.d: a symptom of allergic states; increased eosinophils in the blood
(uncountable) The condition of having a high concentration of eosinophils (eosinophil granulocytes) in the blood.

eosinophilic.e:

Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der.
Latin -o-bor.

From eosin + -o- + -philic.

s.d: of or relating to eosinophil
That is readily stained with eosin.
Of, pertaining to an eosinophil or to eosinophilia.
